text:
Swiss renewable energy firm Axpo has completed its first ship-to-ship liquid biomethane (bio-LNG) operation in the Port of Barcelona, Spain.

Japan-based energy transport company Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) fuelled its vehicle carrier using bio-LNG from Axpo’s 7,500m³ small-scale bunkering vessel, supporting low-carbon fuel integration in Mediterranean maritime infrastructure.

This builds on Axpo’s existing western European supply partnership with MOL, expanding bio-LNG distribution in the Mediterranean from bunkering sites in Málaga and Barcelona.

The operation marks Axpo’s third successful bio-LNG operation in a major Spanish port, with a license to operate in the Port of Valencia.

Daniele Corti, Head of Small-Scale LNG at Axpo, said, “We’re proving that alternative marine fuels can be operationally reliable [and] a critical stepping stone in the maritime industry’s transition to a lower-carbon future.”

Research and consultancy firm Wood Mackenzie expects bio-LNG demand from the shipping industry to exceed half of Europe’s biomethane production capacity by 2050.

Set to begin in 2027, the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has approved a fuel standard and pricing mechanism for greenhouse gas emissions to reach its net-zero emission goal set for around 2050.

The World Biogas Association (WBA) recently reported global biomethane production will need to reach six to 12 billion cubic metres (bcm) by 2030 and 20bcm to 40bcm by 2035 to meet stringent IMO and FuelEU standards.

Bio-LNG is produced primarily from renewable biomass, offering a lower-carbon fuel for maritime operations.

text:
Kvasir Technologies announced that it has raised €10 million in Series A financing to accelerate the scale-up and commercialization of its climate-neutral marine fuel.

European Energy joined the round as a new investor and strategic partner, alongside existing investors EIFO, Mærsk Growth, and Footprint Fund.

The financing will support the development and design of a new commercial production plant and help scale Kvasir Technologies’ climate-neutral drop-in fuel for use in existing vessels.

Kvasir Technologies is a Danish biofuel startup and spin-out from research at the Technical University of Denmark. The company has developed technology that converts non-edible lignin-based residues from agriculture and forestry into refined biofuels for shipping.

The company said its biofuel can serve as an immediate replacement for fossil marine fuel without requiring modifications to ship engines or changes to existing infrastructure.

As part of the partnership, European Energy and Kvasir Technologies are establishing KVEEN Biofuels, which is working toward the construction of a commercial-scale plant using Kvasir Technologies’ patented technology.

The new funding will also support scale-up work at Kvasir Technologies’ test facility in Fredericia, Denmark, which can produce up to 2 tonnes of biofuel per day.

Development work will also begin on the company’s first commercial plant in Aabenraa in southern Jutland. The plant is expected to demonstrate the technology at industrial scale.

Kvasir Technologies said the investment comes during a challenging funding environment for climate tech startups, but the company attracted investor support due to the maturity of its technology, commercial prospects, and path to commercialization.

“This investment round enables us to take the next crucial steps in developing and scaling our technology. At the same time, it underlines that there is still strong support for solutions that can deliver real climate impact in the maritime sector.”

Joachim Bachmann Nielsen, CEO of Kvasir Technologies

“What will be decisive for Kvasir’s technology is that, through innovation and scaling, we achieve attractive price points for customers and thereby secure long-term offtake agreements before construction begins. We have some experience with that process and look forward to the collaboration.”

Knud Erik Andersen, CEO of European Energy

“With European Energy, we gain a partner with proven experience in developing and financing energy infrastructure at scale. This reduces the risk of our first commercial plant and accelerates our route to market.”

Ulrik Falkenberg Lending, CCO of Kvasir Technologies

“Kvasir Technologies represents a technological solution with strong potential to reduce CO2 emissions in one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize. The combination of scalable technology, a biofuel that can be used in existing fleets and strong partnerships makes the case particularly attractive.”

text:
CMB.TECH NV and Fortescue have entered into a landmark agreement to accelerate the transition towards cleaner and more sustainable maritime transportation through the deployment of ammonia-capable bulk carriers. The partnership involves the long-term charter of up to 12 Newcastlemax dry bulk vessels, each with a carrying capacity of approximately 210,000 deadweight tonnes (dwt), from Bocimar, the dry bulk shipping division of CMB.TECH. The agreement represents a major milestone in the shipping industry’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and promote the use of ammonia as a next-generation carbon-free marine fuel.

As part of the agreement, three of the 12 Newcastlemax vessels will be delivered with advanced dual-fuel engines capable of operating on both conventional marine fuels and ammonia. These vessels are expected to commence operations by the end of 2026, demonstrating the immediate application of ammonia-based propulsion technology in large-scale commercial shipping. The remaining nine vessels will be constructed as ammonia-ready ships, allowing them to be retrofitted with ammonia engines in the future as fuel infrastructure, technology, and global availability of green ammonia continue to expand.

The adoption of green ammonia as a marine fuel has the potential to significantly reduce the environmental impact of the shipping sector. According to estimates, if the entire fleet operates using green ammonia, the vessels could collectively lower carbon dioxide emissions by nearly 250,000 tonnes annually compared with traditional fossil-based marine fuels. This reduction highlights the significant role that alternative fuels can play in supporting the maritime industry’s broader decarbonisation goals and international climate commitments.

Katie Charuga, Director of Integrated Operations at Fortescue, emphasized that the global shipping industry must move beyond discussions and take practical steps toward reducing emissions. She stated that green ammonia offers one of the most promising and realistic pathways for cutting carbon emissions from ocean transport. The agreement with CMB.TECH reflects Fortescue’s commitment to investing in innovative technologies and collaborating with partners who are actively working toward a zero-emission shipping future.

Charuga further highlighted the success of Fortescue’s Green Pioneer demonstration vessel, which has already proven that ammonia can be used safely and effectively in maritime operations. She noted that the next major challenge is scaling this technology across commercial fleets. Through the investment in ammonia-capable bulk carriers, Fortescue aims to stimulate demand for green ammonia, encourage further development of supporting infrastructure, and accelerate the adoption of cleaner fuel technologies throughout the shipping industry.

Alexander Saverys, Chief Executive Officer of CMB.TECH, stated that the company’s long-standing relationship with Fortescue, spanning more than two decades through Bocimar, is built on mutual trust, shared sustainability ambitions, and a commitment to transforming maritime transport. He described the agreement as a strong demonstration that ammonia can become a commercially viable and effective fuel solution for the global shipping industry.

Saverys also stressed that the collaboration sends a powerful message to the maritime sector at a time when questions remain about the speed and feasibility of shipping decarbonisation. According to him, large-scale emission reductions are achievable when industry leaders are willing to invest in innovative technologies and form partnerships focused on practical implementation rather than future promises.

Overall, the Fortescue-CMB.TECH agreement marks a significant advancement in the development of zero-emission shipping. By combining ammonia-capable vessel technology with the future supply of green ammonia fuel, the partnership aims to accelerate the transformation of global maritime logistics and contribute to a more sustainable, low-carbon shipping industry.

The agreement between Fortescue and CMB.TECH to deploy 12 ammonia-capable Newcastlemax bulk carriers is expected to have a positive long-term impact on the green ammonia value chain and the broader maritime fuel market. The move strengthens confidence in ammonia as a viable zero-carbon shipping fuel and is likely to accelerate investments in green ammonia production, storage infrastructure, and related technologies. Increased adoption of ammonia-powered vessels could create a new demand segment beyond its traditional applications in fertilizers and industrial chemicals.

From a market perspective, the immediate impact on conventional ammonia prices tracked by ChemAnalyst is expected to remain limited, as the vessels will gradually enter service from 2026 onward and large-scale green ammonia consumption will take time to develop. However, in the medium to long term, rising demand from the shipping sector could tighten global ammonia supply, particularly for low-carbon and renewable ammonia grades, leading to upward pressure on green ammonia prices.

text:
Manila: The Philippines is looking to accelerate its bioenergy transition by supporting a higher biodiesel blending mandate, a move aimed at reducing fuel costs, strengthening energy security and creating greater value for the country’s coconut sector.

The Department of Agriculture (DA) has endorsed a proposal to raise the current biodiesel blend level from three percent to five percent, positioning the shift as part of broader efforts to expand the country’s use of renewable energy and locally sourced biofuels.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said he supports a policy resolution submitted by the Philippine Council for Agriculture and Fisheries (PCAF), which recommends an immediate transition to B5 biodiesel.

The recommendation, put forward by PCAF’s National Sectoral Committee on Coconut, comes as fuel prices remain elevated. While the advisory body noted that the measure is not an immediate solution to fuel costs, it said a higher blend of coconut-based biodiesel could improve fuel mileage over time and gradually reduce fuel expenses for motorists.

The transition to B5 had originally been scheduled for October this year but remains uncertain as the country continues to operate under the current B3 blending requirement.

Last year, the Department of Energy suspended implementation of B4 and B5 following a recommendation from the National Biofuels Board after global coconut oil prices surged sharply.

Coconut oil is the primary feedstock used to produce coco methyl ester (CME), which is blended with diesel to create biodiesel. Compared with conventional diesel, CME offers lower sulfur emissions and reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

The Department of Agriculture said market conditions have improved and now support not only lifting the suspension but also advancing implementation of the higher biodiesel blend.

According to Tiu Laurel, expanding demand for CME could generate stronger returns for up to 3.5 million coconut farmers while increasing utilisation across the domestic coconut industry.

He added that greater biodiesel adoption would strengthen the country’s energy independence by reducing dependence on imported fuel and increasing the use of renewable domestic resources.

The agriculture department confirmed that the proposal has been submitted to Senator Kiko Pangilinan, chair of the Senate committee on agriculture, food and agrarian reform, and Energy Secretary Sharon Garin.

Under the Biofuels Act, fuel suppliers are required to incorporate locally sourced biofuels into transport fuels to reduce import dependence and support the domestic coconut industry.

The Philippines introduced a one-percent biodiesel blend in 2007, increased it to two percent in 2011 and expanded it to the current three-percent level in 2024.

Australian iron ore giant Fortescue has signed an agreement with Belgian maritime giant CMB.Tech to charter up to 12 ammonia-capable vessels, a significant step in the company’s efforts to scale the decarbonisation of global shipping and advance the adoption of ammonia as a shipping fuel.

Up to three of the 12 vessels – measuring 210,000 deadweight tonnage (dwt) – will be delivered with dual-fuel ammonia engines and are expected to enter service by the end of 2026, while nine other vessels will be ammonia-ready, able to be converted to operate on ammonia in the future.

“The shipping industry doesn’t need more talk. It needs action,” said Katie Charuga, Fortescue director of integrated operations.

“Green ammonia is one of the clearest pathways to reducing carbon dioxide emissions from shipping, and these vessels represent a practical step towards that future. By backing new technologies and working with partners who are prepared to lead, we can help drive the uptake of green ammonia in shipping.

Charuga said that Fortescue’s Green Pioneer demonstration vessel – which has travelled the world and attended key climate and renewable conferences – has already shown that ammonia can be used safely and effectively in marine operations. The next challenge is scaling the use of green ammonia.

“By investing in ammonia-capable vessels and working with partners who share our ambition, we are helping create demand for green ammonia and supporting the technologies needed to reduce emissions from global shipping,” she said.

Fortescue’s Green Pioneer was the world’s first ammonia capable dual-fuel vessel and has served as a visual demonstration not only of Fortescue’s ‘Real Zero’ decarbonisation efforts, but of the role that green ammonia can play in the decarbonisation of global shipping.

The Green Pioneer conducted the world’s first use of ammonia as a marine fuel in early 2024.

Green Pioneer has since sailed internationally, bunkered ammonia, trained crews, and demonstrated the potential value of ammonia-powered propulsion under real-world conditions.

“It also sends a powerful signal to the market, particularly at a time when there is doubt about the decarbonisation of shipping: our sector can decarbonise at scale. It just takes like-minded, determined partners who walk the talk.”

text:
Two new liquefied hydrogen fuel cell-powered bulk carriers are among 10 zero-emission ships and new shore-charging infrastructure that received a total of Nkr1.2Bn (US$124M) in funding from Norway’s Enova SF.

Bergen-based LH2 Shipping secured Nrk344.3M (US$35.5M) in funding in mid-June to build the two liquid hydrogen-powered shortsea bulk carriers and has now received Nrk800M (US$82M) from the Norwegian government agency to support the development and construction of six zero-emissions vessels.

LH2 Shipping chief executive, Ivan Østvik, said the award strengthens the company’s “position as a developer of liquid hydrogen-based zero-emission vessel solutions and brings us yet another step closer to our ambition of enabling a substantial fleet of hydrogen-powered vessels that can help establish a complete maritime liquid hydrogen value chain.”

Founded in 2023, the Norwegian start-up develops a wide range of vessel types that deploy liquid hydrogen (LH2) power, most notably serving as the project lead for Norled’s MF Hydra, the world’s first hydrogen fuel cell-powered ferry. The groundbreaking ferry has been in operation for five years, providing valuable technical, operational, and regulatory learnings for this and other liquid hydrogen vessel projects.

Zero-emission sailing all year round

As revealed by LH2 Shipping, these vessels for the Strandbulk Project will have hydrogen-powered proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells. The 7,700-dwt shortsea bulk carriers will transport dry and general cargo mainly in Norway and the Baltic region. For propulsion, the 108.2-m ships will have onboard hydrogen systems consisting of a 17-tonne LH2 storage tank and 3,400 kW of PEM fuel cells. A 3 MWh battery pack will be installed to support the fuel cells, storing energy and providing zero-emission operation capability while in port. Shore power systems will allow connection to local electricity grids during loading and unloading operations. Each bulk carrier will have a standby diesel generator, offering the option to sail on marine diesel or biodiesel if the LH2 supply fails or is not in place at the time when the ships are delivered from the shipyard.

LH2 Shipping expects the StrandBulk vessel design to be 30% more energy efficient than similar vessels, using an optimised hull, energy-saving technologies, energy management systems, and even solar panels on the cargo hatches.

A further 22 zero-emission vessels are already under construction and planned for operation in Norwegian waters.

text:
Achieving climate targets requires all sectors, including shipping, to undergo a transition. Significant funding is being provided for vessels powered by batteries, ammonia and hydrogen, marking an important step towards making zero-emission solutions increasingly available for the maritime sector.

Enova plays a key role in supporting the transformation of an industry responsible for eight per cent of Norway’s emissions, said Climate and Environment Minister Andreas Bjelland Eriksen.

Enova is a state enterprise owned by the Ministry of Climate and Environment. The purpose of Enova and the Climate and Energy Fund is to contribute to meeting Norway’s climate commitments and to promote effective climate and energy transition measures on the path to a low-emission society.

Of the ten new zero-emission vessels receiving support from Enova, six will be battery-powered, two will run on hydrogen and two on ammonia. In addition, one of the projects will receive support for charging infrastructure. Payments will only be made once costs have been incurred and documented.

The aim of the ten projects that Enova is supporting with NOK 1.3 billion is to demonstrate that batteries, hydrogen and ammonia can become competitive solutions as maritime transport moves towards significantly larger emissions reductions than today

…said Acting CEO of Enova, Rune Holmen.

Accelerating the transition

According to DNV, there are 3,785 vessels operating in domestic traffic in Norway. Of these, 112 are zero-emission vessels, representing around three per cent of the fleet. Norway currently has the highest share of zero-emission ships in the world.

However, new data from Enova shows that at the current pace of transition, Norway is unlikely to meet its target of achieving zero greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport by 2050.

A further 22 zero-emission vessels are already under construction and planned for operation in Norwegian waters. With the ten new projects now receiving funding, the transition of the maritime sector will accelerate, although zero-emission technologies remain in an early stage of development.

Electric vessels and charging infrastructure

Several of the supported projects will demonstrate how greater electrification can be achieved in maritime transport. Seistar will receive funding for a fully electric processing vessel and charging facilities, enabling emissions-free transport and processing of fish between aquaculture sites and processing plants. Watt Goodfish will receive support for two similar electric vessels.

Eitzen Avanti will receive funding for two new battery-electric container vessels. Together with two vessels that received support last year, they could form a new zero-emission container transport system between Norway and Europe. Construction of the two previously supported vessels has now been approved, with operations planned from 2029.

The vessels will be equipped with battery systems exceeding 100 MWh, making them the largest ship battery systems in the world. Nordic Sea Concept will receive support to build a fully electric cruise vessel for operation in Norwegian fjords. The vessel will be equipped with a large 20 MWh battery system.

Making zero-emission investment easier

For hydrogen and ammonia, the funding will also help establish the first functioning supply chains for zero-emission fuels in the maritime sector. LH2 Shipping will receive support for two bulk carriers powered by liquid hydrogen, while Bergen Tankers will develop two ammonia-powered tankers for Equinor.

We have already supported ammonia bunkering facilities, as well as hydrogen production and refuelling. As more ships now receive support, it is essential that production, distribution, bunkering and use of new fuels develop simultaneously. Once the first supply chains are established, it will become easier for more actors to invest in zero-emission technology

…said Rune Holmen.

On 15 June, another development emerged for the future of ammonia-powered vessels. Azane Infrastructure AS, which received Enova support last year to build three ammonia bunkering facilities, has committed to paying a penalty if the projects are not completed.

The Enova funding was provided through the “Ammonia Bunkering Facilities” programme. The three facilities will be built at the offshore ports of Mongstad, Risavika and Fjordbase.

Together, the projects supported by Enova are expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 46,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually. This is equivalent to the yearly emissions from around 18,000 diesel passenger cars.

The direct emissions reductions created by our support for zero-emission maritime vessels are a positive additional effect. The most important impact is that these projects pave the way for a broader transformation of the maritime sector, enabling significant and lasting reductions in emissions.

text:
The Hidden Carbon Cost Embedded in Every Tonne of Iron Ore Shipped Across the Pacific

Before a single tonne of iron ore reaches a blast furnace in China, Japan, or South Korea, it has already accumulated a significant carbon liability simply by existing on a ship. The vessels responsible for moving bulk commodities across oceanic trade routes are, by cumulative fuel burn, among the most emissions-intensive transport assets on the planet. A single large bulk carrier burning heavy fuel oil on the Pilbara-to-Asia corridor can consume hundreds of tonnes of fuel per day, generating thousands of tonnes of CO₂ over the course of a round trip.

For companies whose entire business model depends on repeating that voyage hundreds of times annually, the decarbonisation of marine transport is not a distant policy consideration. It is an operational reality with an accelerating compliance deadline attached to it.

That is the context in which Fortescue's (ASX: FMG) commitment to Fortescue ammonia-capable vessels needs to be understood. Not as a marketing exercise, but as a structurally motivated response to one of the most technically complex emissions challenges in global heavy industry.

Why Bulk Iron Ore Shipping Sits at the Intersection of Scale and Emissions Intensity

The iron ore trade between Western Australia and Northeast Asia is one of the highest-frequency, highest-volume commodity shipping corridors in the world. Newcastlemax and Capesize vessels operate on this route in near-continuous rotation, and the cumulative fuel consumption across an entire fleet over a calendar year runs into millions of tonnes of marine fuel.

The International Maritime Organisation's revised 2023 greenhouse gas strategy sets out legally binding reduction milestones that make this fuel consumption problem urgent rather than theoretical:

A minimum 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by 2030, measured against 2008 baseline levels

A further reduction of at least 70% by 2040

Net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050

For a company like Fortescue, which ships hundreds of millions of tonnes of iron ore annually, these targets translate directly into fleet technology decisions that need to be made now, not in 2040. Vessel construction lead times, retrofit scheduling windows, and bunkering infrastructure development all operate on timelines of five to fifteen years. Decisions deferred become options foreclosed.

Understanding Why Ammonia Emerged as Fortescue's Fuel of Choice

The alternative marine fuel landscape is crowded with contenders, each carrying distinct trade-offs across emissions profile, energy density, infrastructure maturity, and cost. Understanding why Fortescue converged on ammonia as its primary decarbonisation pathway requires examining how the leading alternatives compare.

Marine Fuel Alternative Carbon Content Energy Density (MJ/kg) Commercial Maturity (2026) LNG High (fossil origin) ~50 Fully commercial Methanol Low to moderate ~20 Early commercial Green Hydrogen Zero ~120 Pre-commercial Green Ammonia Zero ~18.6 Demonstrator / early commercial Biofuels Variable ~37 Niche commercial

Ammonia's defining characteristic is structural: the molecule NH₃ contains no carbon atoms. Combustion therefore produces no CO₂ as a direct byproduct. When the ammonia is itself produced using renewable electricity to power an electrolysis process, the full lifecycle emissions can approach near-zero, making it one of the very few marine fuels theoretically capable of satisfying the IMO's 2050 net-zero mandate without relying on carbon offsets. Furthermore, this connects directly to broader efforts in green iron production, where decarbonising the entire supply chain — from mine to steelmill — is increasingly the central strategic objective.

LNG, by contrast, reduces CO₂ emissions by approximately 20 to 25% compared to heavy fuel oil but delivers no pathway to the deep decarbonisation the IMO targets require. Companies that have committed heavily to LNG as a transitional fuel may find themselves needing to transition again within the same asset lifecycle, a prospect that concentrates capital risk rather than reducing it.

Fortescue's decision to bypass LNG as a bridge fuel and move directly toward ammonia-capable vessels represents a higher-risk, higher-conviction strategic position, one that bets on the technology maturing before the regulatory and competitive penalties for inaction become prohibitive.

The Technical Architecture of Ammonia-Capable Propulsion at Sea

Pure ammonia combustion presents genuine engineering challenges. Ammonia has a narrow flammability range, a high auto-ignition temperature, and combustion characteristics that differ substantially from conventional marine diesel. The solution Fortescue has adopted, in common with engine manufacturers developing the technology, is a dual-fuel configuration that uses ammonia as the primary energy carrier while a small quantity of diesel or pilot fuel initiates and stabilises the combustion cycle.

This approach is technically significant for several reasons:

It eliminates the need to solve pure ammonia ignition at commercial scale before deployment

It preserves operational redundancy, as vessels can revert to conventional fuel operation if required

It allows ammonia percentage in the fuel blend to be progressively increased as engine technology and crew competency develop

It reduces the capital risk of early adoption by avoiding an all-or-nothing technology commitment

The dual-fuel approach does, however, introduce one important byproduct challenge. Ammonia combustion generates elevated levels of nitrogen oxides (NOx), a regulated air pollutant under IMO Tier III standards. Managing this requires Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) after-treatment systems to bring NOx output within compliance thresholds, adding engineering complexity and cost to the propulsion package.

A related technical concern is ammonia slip, where trace quantities of uncombusted ammonia pass through the combustion cycle and exit via exhaust. Beyond the direct air quality implications, ammonia slip can contribute indirectly to nitrous oxide (N₂O) formation, itself a potent greenhouse gas. Engine manufacturers including MAN Energy Solutions and Wärtsilä are actively developing low-slip combustion solutions specifically for the ammonia fuel context, with commercial-scale availability expected to align with the industry's 2030 retrofit timelines.

The Green Pioneer: What the World's First Commercial Ammonia Vessel Demonstrator Proved

The Fortescue Green Pioneer occupies a unique position in maritime history as the world's first dual-fuel ammonia-powered vessel to conduct operational demonstrations at commercial scale across multiple international ports. Two of the vessel's four engines were converted to dual-fuel ammonia-diesel capability, preserving the redundancy necessary for safe blue-water operation while demonstrating the technology under real-world conditions.

The strategic choice of demonstration ports carries as much significance as the technology itself. The Green Pioneer completed ammonia bunkering and operational demonstrations at Singapore, Southampton, Boston, and New York. Each of these locations represents a major global maritime hub:

Singapore is the world's largest bunkering port by volume, and its inclusion signals ammonia's potential to penetrate the global marine fuel supply chain at scale

Southampton provides access to European regulatory frameworks and Lloyd's Register classification infrastructure

Boston and New York engage the United States Coast Guard and American Bureau of Shipping regulatory ecosystem, broadening the evidentiary base for ammonia fuel acceptance

This multi-jurisdictional demonstration approach is not incidental. Classification societies, flag states, and port authorities each operate under different regulatory frameworks, and building an evidence base across all of them simultaneously accelerates the development of the unified international standards that commercial-scale ammonia shipping will require.

How an Ammonia Dual-Fuel Vessel Operates: A Step-by-Step Breakdown

Ammonia bunkering at port — Liquid ammonia is transferred to the vessel via specialist equipment under stringent safety protocols, stored in either cryogenic or pressurised onboard tanks depending on the vessel's storage system design

Engine and fuel system preparation — Dual-fuel engine management systems are calibrated to the target ammonia-diesel blend ratio for the voyage profile

Combustion initiation — Diesel pilot injection creates the ignition conditions required, after which ammonia provides the dominant energy contribution across the combustion cycle

Emissions monitoring underway — Onboard systems track NOx, CO₂, SOx, and ammonia slip in real time, generating the compliance data required for IMO Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating assessments

Port arrival and data submission — Accumulated emissions records are submitted to classification society auditors and used to inform ongoing regulatory framework development

From Demonstrator to Commercial Scale: The CMB.TECH Charter and Fleet Expansion

The demonstrator phase of Fortescue's ammonia vessel programme has produced a technically validated proof of concept. The next challenge is translating that proof of concept into commercial-scale deployment across vessels large enough to carry meaningful iron ore cargo volumes.

Fortescue's agreement with CMB.TECH, the clean marine technology division of Compagnie Maritime Belge, addresses this directly. The charter agreement covers the deployment of a 210,000 deadweight tonne Newcastlemax ore carrier configured as a dual-fuel ammonia-capable newbuild, with delivery expected by the end of 2026.

CMB.TECH is among the most technically advanced commercial operators currently developing ammonia-fuelled bulk carriers, making the partnership a capability combination rather than a simple charter arrangement. Fortescue brings the operational demand signal and the decarbonisation strategic commitment; CMB.TECH brings the vessel engineering expertise and newbuild delivery pipeline.

Fortescue's Ammonia Vessel Milestone Timeline

Period Key Development Pre-2024 Green Pioneer converted to dual-fuel ammonia-diesel configuration 2024–2025 Operational demonstrations at Singapore, Southampton, Boston, and New York 2026 (expected delivery) 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax ammonia-capable ore carrier via CMB.TECH/Bocimar By 2030 Fleet-wide retrofit of Fortescue-owned vessels with ammonia-capable engines Post-2030 Ammonia propulsion specified as standard for all future Fortescue newbuilds

The choice of the Newcastlemax vessel class for the first commercial deployment is deliberate and technically significant. At approximately 200,000 to 210,000 dwt, these are the largest bulk carriers capable of transiting Newcastle Harbour in Australia and are purpose-optimised for the Pilbara-to-Asia iron ore corridor. Demonstrating ammonia propulsion at this scale, rather than on a smaller vessel, provides the maritime industry with a commercially representative data set that smaller demonstrators cannot replicate.

Competitive Positioning: How Fortescue's Strategy Compares Across Major Bulk Shippers

Fortescue's ammonia-first approach stands in contrast to the strategies adopted by other major bulk commodity operators, most of whom have chosen LNG as a transitional fuel while monitoring alternative fuel development from a safer technological distance. In addition, the broader context of the China steel and iron ore market adds further urgency to these decisions, as the region's demand trajectory heavily influences how quickly decarbonisation solutions must be scaled.

Company Primary Fuel Strategy Fleet Status (2026) Fortescue (ASX: FMG) Green ammonia, direct pathway Demonstrator operational; Newcastlemax delivery 2026; fleet retrofit by 2030 BHP (ASX: BHP) LNG transitional, green methanol long-term LNG vessels in service; methanol trials underway Rio Tinto (ASX: RIO) Wind-assisted propulsion, LNG Rotor sail trials active; LNG newbuilds ordered Vale (Brazil) LNG and biofuels Large LNG-capable Valemax fleet operational

The contrast is instructive. BHP and Rio Tinto's LNG commitments reduce near-term emissions but do not solve the 2050 challenge. Their strategies effectively purchase time while technology matures. Fortescue's ammonia commitment accepts greater near-term technology risk in exchange for a theoretically more direct path to the deep decarbonisation outcome that global shipping regulations will eventually require.

Whether that bet proves prescient or premature depends substantially on factors outside any single company's control, including green ammonia production costs, bunkering infrastructure development, and the pace of regulatory standardisation.

The Infrastructure Gap: Why Port Readiness is the Critical Bottleneck

Vessel technology is only half of the ammonia shipping equation. A dual-fuel ammonia vessel without access to ammonia bunkering at its ports of call is operationally constrained regardless of its engineering sophistication.

Unlike LNG, which has benefited from a decade of deliberate global bunkering network investment, ammonia marine bunkering infrastructure remains in its infancy as of 2026. The number of ports globally that have conducted ship-to-ship or terminal-to-ship ammonia fuel transfers for marine propulsion purposes can be counted on one hand.

Port authorities face a specific set of requirements before ammonia bunkering can be offered commercially:

Development and approval of Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) protocols specific to ammonia fuel transfer operations

Certification of bunkering equipment and transfer hoses rated for ammonia service conditions

Training and certification of port personnel in ammonia emergency response procedures

Establishment of exclusion zone protocols and evacuation procedures given ammonia's acute toxicity

Ammonia is acutely toxic to humans at concentrations of approximately 300 parts per million and above, creating a safety profile meaningfully different from LNG or methanol. This is not an insurmountable challenge, given that ammonia has been handled industrially at scale for over a century in fertiliser production and refrigeration applications, but it requires purpose-built protocols that the maritime industry is still developing.

Regulatory Complexity: The Patchwork of Standards Ammonia Shipping Must Navigate

The IMO's International Code of Safety for Ships Using Gases or Other Low-Flashpoint Fuels (IGF Code) is the primary regulatory framework governing alternative marine fuel vessels, and it is being progressively amended to incorporate ammonia. Operational data generated by the Green Pioneer's demonstration programme is actively informing this amendment process, giving Fortescue an unusual degree of influence over the regulatory standards that will govern its own future fleet.

Classification societies have each published interim guidelines for ammonia-fuelled vessels:

Lloyd's Register has issued interim rules for ammonia-fuelled ships covering fuel system design, safety systems, and risk assessment requirements

DNV has published its ammonia-fuelled vessel class notation framework, including requirements for NOx after-treatment and ammonia detection systems

Bureau Veritas has similarly issued interim guidance covering structural and systems requirements for ammonia fuel storage and distribution aboard vessels

A unified international standard remains under development, creating a compliance complexity challenge for vessels operating across multiple flag state jurisdictions simultaneously. This regulatory fragmentation is itself a market inefficiency that early movers like Fortescue are positioned to help resolve by generating the operational data that standard-setters require.

Green Ammonia Supply: The Upstream Dependency That Determines Everything

The environmental case for ammonia-fuelled shipping rests entirely on one foundational assumption: that the ammonia being consumed was produced using renewable energy. Green ammonia, produced via electrolysis powered by wind or solar electricity, delivers a near-zero lifecycle emissions profile. Grey ammonia, produced via steam methane reforming of natural gas, offers no meaningful climate benefit compared to conventional marine fuel.

This upstream dependency is the most important and least discussed aspect of the ammonia shipping transition. A vessel technically capable of burning ammonia but supplied with grey ammonia at port is not contributing to decarbonisation in any meaningful sense. The emissions reduction is occurring on paper, not in the atmosphere.

Fortescue's broader corporate strategy includes large-scale green hydrogen and green ammonia production through its energy business division, creating a potential vertical integration pathway from renewable electricity generation through to vessel bunkering. Innovations in hydrogen iron ore reduction are closely related, as both pathways depend on scaling green hydrogen infrastructure to commercially viable cost levels. Furthermore, Australia's green metals leadership position provides a structural advantage in developing green ammonia supply chains at the scale maritime shipping would require.

The strategic coherence of Fortescue's position is notable: if the company can successfully develop domestic green ammonia production at competitive cost, it simultaneously solves its own fleet's fuel supply challenge and potentially creates an export commodity in green ammonia that serves other shipping operators globally.

This demand-anchor dynamic extends beyond Fortescue's own balance sheet. By committing to Fortescue ammonia-capable vessels at commercial scale before industry consensus has formed, the company is generating the demand signal that justifies infrastructure investment by:

Electrolyser manufacturers scaling production capacity and reducing unit costs

Port operators making the business case for ammonia bunkering facility capital expenditure

Shipyards developing standardised ammonia-capable vessel designs for the broader bulk carrier market

Insurance markets developing actuarial frameworks for ammonia-fuelled vessel coverage

Frequently Asked Questions About Fortescue Ammonia-Capable Vessels

What exactly are Fortescue ammonia-capable vessels?

Fortescue ammonia-capable vessels are bulk carriers fitted with dual-fuel engine systems capable of burning a blend of ammonia and diesel for propulsion, rather than relying solely on conventional heavy fuel oil. The Green Pioneer is the operational demonstrator, while a 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax vessel represents the first commercial-scale deployment under the CMB.TECH charter arrangement.

Why is ammonia considered zero-carbon as a marine fuel?

Ammonia (NH₃) contains no carbon atoms in its molecular structure, so its combustion produces no CO₂. When produced using renewable electricity, the full supply chain lifecycle emissions approach near-zero, satisfying the IMO's long-term net-zero shipping target without requiring carbon offset mechanisms.

What are the biggest risks to Fortescue's ammonia shipping strategy?

The primary risk factors include the pace of green ammonia production cost reduction, the development of commercial-scale bunkering infrastructure at major ports, the finalisation of unified international regulatory standards for ammonia-fuelled vessels, and the resolution of NOx and ammonia slip technical challenges at the engine level. Each of these represents a genuine uncertainty rather than a solved problem.

When is the new Newcastlemax ammonia vessel expected to enter service?

The 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax ammonia-capable ore carrier developed with CMB.TECH (Bocimar) is expected to be delivered by the end of 2026, representing the transition from demonstrator phase to initial commercial-scale operation.

How does Fortescue's approach differ from BHP and Rio Tinto?

Fortescue has committed directly to ammonia as its primary decarbonisation pathway, bypassing LNG as a transitional fuel. BHP and Rio Tinto have both invested in LNG-capable vessels, which reduce emissions by approximately 20 to 25% compared to heavy fuel oil but do not deliver the deep decarbonisation required to meet 2050 IMO targets without additional interventions. Consequently, the China iron ore outlook may increasingly favour suppliers who can demonstrate credible green shipping credentials as regulatory pressure intensifies.

Key Considerations for Evaluating the Long-Term Significance of This Programme

Several dimensions of Fortescue's ammonia vessel programme deserve consideration from an industry and investment perspective:

Technology timing risk: Committing to ammonia propulsion before unified international standards are finalised creates compliance uncertainty as regulations evolve around an already-deployed fleet

Supply chain dependency: The decarbonisation outcome is contingent on green ammonia supply being available at commercial scale and competitive cost at ports on the Pilbara-to-Asia trade route

Regulatory influence: Fortescue's early mover position gives the company disproportionate influence over the international regulatory frameworks being developed, a strategic asset not reflected on any balance sheet

Market-making potential: If Fortescue's programme successfully validates ammonia shipping at commercial scale, the template becomes available to the entire bulk commodity shipping sector, potentially accelerating adoption in ways that extend Fortescue's first-mover advantage into a market-shaping role

Independent assessment of investment decisions is recommended.

text:
Australian mining giant Fortescue will charter 12 ammonia-ready cargo ships from Belgian maritime group CMB.Tech, with three dual-fuel ammonia-powered vessels set to enter operation this year.

The remaining nine will require conversion to run on ammonia, though no timeline for this or their service entry has been revealed.

The vessels, 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax bulk carriers from CMB’s dry bulk division Bocimar, will be chartered by Fortescue.

According to CMB, the fleet will help stimulate demand for green ammonia and could eliminate around 250,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually if fuelled by the molecule.

Alexander Saverys, CEO of CMB, said the deployments will showcase ammonia’s viability as a marine fuel and send a “powerful signal to the market.”

“At a time when there is doubt about the decarbonisation of shipping, our sector can decarbonise at scale,” he added.

It follows the pair joining forces in 2025 to develop an iron ore carrier, as well as numerous rollouts of CMB-developed ammonia-fuelled boats.

In March 2025, the maritime group partnered with Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) to deploy nine further ammonia-powered vessels between 2026 and 2029. It was also involved in the 1,400 TEU Yara Eyde container ship set to begin fertiliser deliveries this year.

Ammonia continues to be slated as a key future fuel for shipping. However, while carbon-free, it faces criticisms around its toxicity and NOx emissions, both significant environmental concerns.

It comes as green hydrogen proponents hope the International Maritime Organization (IMO) will be able to secure the votes to pass a global carbon price on shippers, which had been postponed last year after protests by major economies.

The measure, which is widely viewed as tool to unlock demand for green hydrogen-based fuels, had been criticised for its potential to increase prices for shippers and end-users.

A new vote is expected to be held in October.

text:
"We're in a hurry trying to identify which fuels shipping must use to become climate neutral by 2050."

So says Anders Erlandsson, a maritime professor at DTU Construct and affiliated with DTU Maritime Center.

Even after many years of global research into green alternatives, there is still no convincing candidate ready to replace shipping fossil fuels, explains Anders Erlandsson.

Nor does it help in the green transition of shipping that it currently lacks broad international support. In the autumn of 2025, a majority in the UN's shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization (IMO), voted to pause negotiations on the 2050 target for a year.

Must be ready by 2030

But it's urgent to find solutions that can lower shipping's carbon emissions, because if the entire global fleet is to be converted to climate neutrality by 2050, the shipping companies must know which solutions to invest in no later than in four years, says Anders Erlandsson, who elaborates:

"If you convert five per cent of the fleet annually, it will take 20 years to convert the entire fleet. This means that the ships that leave the shipyards already in 2030 must, in principle, be ready for green propulsion if shipping is to be climate neutral by 2050."

But the question remains what the shipping companies should invest in—ammonia engines, methanol, or electricity, to name just some of the many possible solutions. The right solution depends on multiple factors, including the size of the vessel and whether it is an ocean-going vessel or just a ferry that sails in inland waters, says the professor.

"Small vessels can be electrified, but the large ocean-going container vessels cannot, because it requires so many batteries that there will be no room for the containers," says Anders Erlandsson.

Dilemma of biofuels

There is a low-hanging fruit, namely biofuels—i.e. fuels produced from biomass. Biofuels are attractive because they fit the standard fuel specifications, which means they can be used without significant adjustments to, e.g., engines, fuelling, or storage. But biofuels put us in a dilemma, Anders Erlandsson points out:

"If there's insufficient biomass to produce biofuels for the global fleet, then the question is whether it is sustainable for our planet to use land for growing biomass to get enough for fuel. Areas that we may or may not need for food production because they are covered by rainforest. Biomass should therefore be regarded as a limited resource and is probably not suitable to meet shipping demand for energy."

Unrealistic climate targets

Anders Erlandsson predicts that we will see combinations of solutions in the attempt to achieve climate-neutral shipping.

Some will combine green technologies such as sails or power to reduce fossil fuel consumption. Others will combine conventional fuels with fuels that have lower carbon emissions such as bio-based LNG (liquefied natural gas) or biofuels.

Some will exploit carbon capture, and others may again use nuclear power if smaller reactors are developed for this purpose. Either way, we still have a long way to go before we can achieve 100% CO2-neutral shipping, says Anders Erlandsson:

"As things stand, I think it's unrealistic to believe that shipping by 2050 will be 100% climate neutral. My optimistic guess is that by 2050 the ships may be 80 per cent climate neutral."

text:
Hong Kong’s Marine Department (MD) will introduce two new incentive schemes from 16 June to encourage greater use of alternative marine fuels.

Both programmes will remain in place for three years.

The Hong Kong government has earmarked around $34 million in this year’s budget to support the initiatives. The funding will be used to offer port dues concessions to vessels powered by or carrying alternative fuels, as well as financial incentives for alternative-fuelled ships registered under the Hong Kong flag.

Under the Port Dues Incentive Scheme for Green Maritime Fuel-related Vessels, rebates will be available to alternative fuel-related ocean-going vessels (OGVs). This includes ships powered by or bunkering approved alternative fuels in Hong Kong, as well as vessels transporting such fuels for local supply.

The approved fuels under the scheme are LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen and B20 biofuel containing at least 20% biofuel. Eligible OGVs carrying out the specified operations during their stay in Hong Kong can apply for reimbursement of 25-50% of the port dues they have paid. The rebate covers charges such as port facilities and light dues, anchorage dues, buoy dues and port clearance permit fees levied under the Shipping and Port Control Regulations.

The MD said the scheme is designed to promote the uptake of alternative fuels, which typically cost more than conventional fuels, while stimulating early demand for green bunkering services in Hong Kong.

“This will in turn attract other players in the green maritime fuel bunkering supply chain, such as bunker suppliers, bunker operators and traders, to establish and expand their operations in Hong Kong. We expect this scheme to attract more than 1,000 visits to Hong Kong by green maritime fuel-related vessels,” an MD spokesperson said.

The second initiative, the Green Vessels Registration Incentive Scheme, aims to attract and retain alternative-fuelled vessels in the Hong Kong Shipping Registry (HKSR).

The scheme is open to both existing and newly registered Hong Kong-flagged ships that use alternative fuels as their primary propulsion fuel. Eligible fuels include LNG, methanol, ammonia and hydrogen, while conventional fuels and biofuels are excluded.

Each qualifying vessel will receive an annual subsidy of HK$60,000 (about $7,600) during the three-year programme. Depending on when a vessel joins and remains in the registry, it may receive support for up to three years, bringing the maximum subsidy per vessel to HK$180,000 (about $23,000).

“We estimate that this scheme will attract approximately 100 vessels powered by green maritime fuels to register with the HKSR,” an MD spokesperson added.

Source: ENGINE

text:
Spanish energy company Repsol on Thursday (18 June) said it has started the commercial supply of co-processed marine fuels with renewable content in the port of Algeciras, one of the main bunkering hubs in the Mediterranean.

The company said this marked the deployment of immediate solutions produced by integrating renewable content directly into conventional refinery processes, supporting the decarbonisation of maritime transport.

Last week, Repsol launched the first commercial voyage of its new generation bunkering vessel Bahía Candela. During this first voyage, the vessel loaded co-processed fuel at Repsol’s Petronor refinery in Bilbao, reinforcing the company’s end-to-end supply capability by integrating refining, logistics, and delivery.

Repsol reportedly chartered the bunkering vessel from shipowner Mureloil.

Designed specifically for marine fuel supply, Bahía Candela features multiproduct capabilities and is prepared to operate with low-emission energy solutions. Its diesel-electric propulsion system and advanced energy storage enable optimised efficiency and reduced emissions during operations.

“This milestone marked Repsol’s entry into the supply of low-carbon marine fuels in Algeciras, leveraging its integrated value chain and expanding its multi-energy offering in the maritime sector, combining conventional products with low-carbon alternatives, thus, strengthening its ability to adapt to the diverse needs of its customers,” Repsol said in a statement.

Co-processing enables the integration of renewable feedstocks, such as oils and residues, alongside conventional streams within refining processes.

This generates fuels with a low-carbon footprint and supports a gradual transition towards solutions that will help to decarbonise the sector, providing a cost-efficient and scalable pathway to supply low-carbon fuels that are fully compatible with existing engines and infrastructure, without requiring changes to vessels or port assets, and using current industrial assets.

Everllence recently announced the successful Type Approval Test (TAT) of its ME-LGIA ammonia-burning engine at its Research Centre Copenhagen (RCC).

Eight classification societies oversaw the testing that took place from 10 to 12 June, marking the latest phase in the engine’s journey towards its market debut.

Bjarne Foldager, Head of Two-Stroke Business, Everllence, said: “The TAT is yet another important step as we definitively move from concept development to seagoing engine operation. It confirms the Everllence B&W ME-LGIA as ready for on-board installation and is the last test before actual sea and gas trials.

“This engine sets new benchmarks in zero-carbon propulsion and digitally connected performance, and has attracted great interest since its development was announced in 2019. It stands testament to Everllence’s unique ability to meet demands and bring innovative fuels to market.”

Everllence officially marketed the ME-LGIA engines at a two-day event in Copenhagen in November 2025. Using the Diesel principle and the well-known, dual-fuel Liquid Gas Injection concept, the engine has a proven track record of several hundred thousand operational hours.

Ole Pyndt Hansen, Senior Vice President, Head of Two-Stroke R&D, Everllence, said: “The TAT is also important in relation to maturing IMO ammonia regulations as it is vital that rules and guidelines are in line with reality to optimise safety onboard vessels.

“This experience comes from industry and the first ammonia-driven ships, which are expected to operate at sea during 2026, will act as compelling input for the development of these guidelines.”

Everllence also noted that the ammonia TAT marked the end of an era with it being the final TAT at the RCC in Copenhagen before the company moves location to outside the city in late-2027.

Published: 22 June, 2026

Verra, a nonprofit organisation that develops and manages the standards for climate and sustainable development, recently released a new methodology in the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) Programme, VM0053 Alternative Low-Carbon Fuels for Shipping, v1.0.

Verra said the methodology provides the first structured, independent accounting framework for quantifying emission reductions in maritime transport, bridging a critical regulatory gap in global trade and enabling the related climate benefits to scale.

VM0053 applies to project activities that involve using low-carbon alternative fuels (e.g., hydrogen produced through water electrolysis, green ammonia, and electro fuels [e-fuels] such as e-LNG, e-LPG, e-diesel, and e-methanol) to replace fossil fuels in shipping.

The methodology applies to new or existing ships, regardless of gross tonnage, operating in territorial or high seas.

Verra added that maritime shipping carries over 80% of global freight and remains a hard-to-abate sector where reducing greenhouse gas emissions has proven to be challenging.

“This methodology helps unlock finance for low-carbon alternative fuels by creating a new revenue stream that can offset the high premium associated with e-fuels,” it said.

“It supports the use of drop-in alternative fuels that can be used to displace fossil fuels in the engines of existing fleets, leveraging these fleets to realise emission reductions. Additionally, this methodology provides a credible mechanism for sourcing, verifying, and scaling reductions in value chain emissions.”

VMD0053 was developed by Iino Kaiun Kaisha, Ltd., Grütter Consulting, and Verra. The methodology underwent public consultation in 2024 as part of Verra’s methodology development process.

text:
Fortescue and CMB.TECH have signed an agreement for the charter of up to 12 ammonia-capable vessels, marking a significant step towards decarbonising global shipping and advancing the adoption of ammonia as a shipping fuel.

Under the agreement, Fortescue will charter a fleet of 12 Newcastlemax dry bulk vessels (210,000 dwt) from Bocimar, CMB.TECH’s dry bulk shipping operator.

Up to three of the vessels will be delivered with dual-fuel ammonia engines and are expected to enter service by the end of 2026. The remaining nine vessels will be ammonia-ready and can be converted to operate on ammonia in the future.

If fuelled by green ammonia, the combined fleet could reduce carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 250,000 tonnes a year compared with conventional marine fuels.

Fortescue Director Integrated Operations, Katie Charuga, said: “The shipping industry doesn’t need more talk. It needs action.

“Green ammonia is one of the clearest pathways to reducing carbon dioxide emissions from shipping, and these vessels represent a practical step towards that future. By backing new technologies and working with partners who are prepared to lead, we can help drive the uptake of green ammonia in shipping.

“Fortescue’s Green Pioneer demonstration vessel has already shown that ammonia can be used safely and effectively in marine operations. The next challenge is scaling the use of green ammonia.

“By investing in ammonia-capable vessels and working with partners who share our ambition, we are helping create demand for green ammonia and supporting the technologies needed to reduce emissions from global shipping.”

CMB.TECH CEO, Alexander Saverys, said: “Fortescue and Bocimar have built a strong partnership over more than two decades, grounded in shared values and a clear commitment to decarbonise shipping.

“This agreement marks an important step in showcasing ammonia as a viable marine fuel and advancing the transition to zero-emission shipping. It also sends a powerful signal to the market, particularly at a time when there is doubt about the decarbonisation of shipping: our sector can decarbonise at scale. It just takes like-minded, determined partners who walk the talk.”

description:
또한, 선박에 카메룬 국기 등록을 사칭하는 웹사이트 두 곳이 적발되어 국내외 당국에 폐쇄 조치를 요청할 예정이다.
마세나 장관은 교통부 조사 결과, 여러 척의 선박이 "현행 법규 및 국제협약을 위반하여 카메룬 국기를 불법적으로 게양하고 해외에서 운항하고 있는 것으로 드러났다"고 밝혔다.
마세나 장관은 언급된 선박 중 일부가 불법 활동에 가담했다고 시사했지만, 서한에는 이러한 활동의 ​​구체적인 내용은 명시되어 있지 않다.
이번 조사에서 마세나 장관은 "카메룬 국내외에 호스팅된 여러 웹사이트들이 카메룬 국적 선박을 사칭하여 등록하고 있는 것으로 드러났다"고 밝혔다.
이는 카메룬 정부가 선박 등록의 투명성을 강화하고 불법 행위에 가담하는 선박으로부터 카메룬 국기를 분리시키려는 노력의 일환이다.
text:
카메룬은 최근 자국 국기를 불법적으로 사용하는 선박에 대한 대대적인 단속에 착수하여 선박 등록부에서 39척의 선박을 삭제하고, 추가로 16척의 선박이 카메룬 국기를 무단으로 게양한 사실을 확인했다.

또한, 선박에 카메룬 국기 등록을 사칭하는 웹사이트 두 곳이 적발되어 국내외 당국에 폐쇄 조치를 요청할 예정이다.

이번 조치는 카메룬의 장 가메룬의 에르네스트 은갈레 비베헤 ​​마세나(Jean Ernest Ngalle Bibehe Massena) 교통부 장관이 국제해사기구(IMO) 사무총장에게 보낸 서한에 명시되어 있으며, 이 서한은 최근 IMO 회원국들에 배포됐다.

마세나 장관은 교통부 조사 결과, 여러 척의 선박이 "현행 법규 및 국제협약을 위반하여 카메룬 국기를 불법적으로 게양하고 해외에서 운항하고 있는 것으로 드러났다"고 밝혔다.

마세나 장관은 언급된 선박 중 일부가 불법 활동에 가담했다고 시사했지만, 서한에는 이러한 활동의 ​​구체적인 내용은 명시되어 있지 않다. 카메룬은 조사 과정에서 문제가 된 선박 목록 두 건을 제출했다.

이번 조사에서 마세나 장관은 "카메룬 국내외에 호스팅된 여러 웹사이트들이 카메룬 국적 선박을 사칭하여 등록하고 있는 것으로 드러났다"고 밝혔다. 구체적으로 언급된 웹사이트는 marinecameroon.com과 cameroonshipregistry.com이다.

두 웹사이트 모두 운영자 파악 및 폐쇄를 위해 관련 국내외 당국에 이관되었다. 마세나 장관은 IMO에 보낸 서한과 같은 날 별도의 서한을 통해 이 사실을 알렸지만, 현재까지는 두 웹사이트 중 한 곳만 폐쇄된 상태라고 밝혔다.

카메룬은 IMO를 통해 두 선박 목록을 배포함으로써, 법적 근거 없이 카메룬 선적을 주장하는 선박에 대해 전 세계 항만국 당국에 경고를 보내는 효과를 거두고 있다.

국제해사법에 따라 선박의 기국은 해당 선박이 적용 가능한 안전 및 규제 기준을 충족하도록 보장할 책임이 있다. 적법한 등록없이 운항하는 선박은 이러한 책임의 적용을 받지 않는다.

이번 회람은 IMO 사무총장에게 회원국 간에 선박 목록이 널리 배포되도록 보장할 것을 요청했다. 이는 카메룬 정부가 선박 등록의 투명성을 강화하고 불법 행위에 가담하는 선박으로부터 카메룬 국기를 분리시키려는 노력의 일환이다.

title: BHP and GCMD launch biofuel trial using used cooking oil and animal waste fats on bulk carrier
description:
Mining major BHP and the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) have launched a pilot project to test lower-emission marine fuels on a BHP-chartered bulk carrier using a biodiesel blend made from used cooking oil (UCO) and waste animal fats.
The biofuel blend is being tested aboard the bulk carrier Berge Lyngor, owned and operated by Berge Bulk, which is transporting BHP iron ore from Western Australia to China.
The companies said that while current shipping biofuel supply depends heavily on used cooking oil, future availability may become constrained.
In this context, biofuels derived from waste animal fats could provide an additional source of lower-emission marine fuel.
Singapore-based GCMD is a non-profit organisation focused on accelerating maritime decarbonisation through pilot projects and technology trials.
text:
Mining major BHP and the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) have launched a pilot project to test lower-emission marine fuels on a BHP-chartered bulk carrier using a biodiesel blend made from used cooking oil (UCO) and waste animal fats.

The trial aims to evaluate how biofuels produced from multiple feedstocks can be blended, handled and deployed under commercial operating conditions while using existing UCO bunkering infrastructure, Oils & Fats International reported.

According to the companies, the pilot will also generate insights into fuel quality, traceability, onboard handling and vessel performance to support wider adoption of alternative marine fuels.

The biofuel blend is being tested aboard the bulk carrier Berge Lyngor, owned and operated by Berge Bulk, which is transporting BHP iron ore from Western Australia to China.

The vessel was bunkered in Singapore in early May with a B100 fuel blend comprising 50 per cent tallow-derived biodiesel supplied by HAMR Energy and 50 per cent used cooking oil methyl ester (UCOME) supplied and blended by Mitsui & Co Energy Trading Singapore (METS).

The companies said operating the vessel on the blend could reduce well-to-wake greenhouse gas emissions by around 79 per cent per voyage compared with conventional very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO).

BHP said the initiative reflects its continued efforts to explore practical pathways for reducing emissions in maritime transport.

Emma Roberts, Vice President – Maritime & Supply Chain Excellence at BHP, said the company intends to continue testing alternative fuels to encourage supply growth and support future investment across the sector.

She noted that with fuel security becoming increasingly important for global trade, expanding opportunities for biofuels will be critical and added that biodiesel, alongside LNG and ammonia, is expected to play an important role in the future marine fuel mix.

The companies said that while current shipping biofuel supply depends heavily on used cooking oil, future availability may become constrained. In this context, biofuels derived from waste animal fats could provide an additional source of lower-emission marine fuel.

The project has received co-funding support from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore under the Maritime Innovation and Technology Fund (MINT).

BHP operates across more than 90 locations globally and produces commodities including iron ore, metallurgical coal and copper. Singapore-based GCMD is a non-profit organisation focused on accelerating maritime decarbonisation through pilot projects and technology trials.

Europe

Rotterdam's B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has declined by only $6/mt over the past week. The limited drop contrasts with a $47/mt fall in conventional VLSFO prices.

Prima Markets assessed POMEME barge price has remained unchanged over the week.

While the sharp decline in VLSFO has weighed on the B30 blend price, a largely unchanged POMEME barge price may have helped cushion the fall.

Gibraltar’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has decreased by around $45/mt. A $32/mt fall in the port’s conventional VLSFO price may have put downward pressure on the blend price.

Meanwhile, Lisbon’s B30-VLSFO price has gained around $20/mt in the past week. The Portuguese port’s B30-VLSFO price is now at a $34/mt price premium over Gibraltar’s, flipping from a discount of $31/mt a week ago.

Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO price has dropped $35/mt to $1,078/mt. The port’s conventional LSMGO price has fallen by a much steeper $136/mt.

Consequently, Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO premium over pure LSMGO has widened by $101/mt in a single week, to $217/mt.

Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO price comes at a $255/mt discount to Lisbon’s B30-LSMGO price, which is at $1,333/mt.

The B30-LSMGO price in Greece’s Piraeus is assessed at $1,292/mt, which is a $214/mt price premium over Rotterdam, and a $41/mt price discount to Lisbon.

Asia

Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has slumped $98/mt in the last week.

The port’s conventional VLSFO price has dropped more modestly, by $41/mt.

Consequently, the B30-VLSFO premium over VLSFO has narrowed by $57/mt during the week.

The Prima-assessed China UCOME cargo price has remained unchanged in the last week. This cargo price is closely connected to Singapore’s biofuel prices as the port is a major importer of Chinese UCOME.

Singapore sold around 1,500 mt/day of bio-bunkers in May, down from around 2,200 mt/day in April, according to the Singapore Maritime & Port Authority’s preliminary data.

Sales of bio-blended bunker fuels fell sharply for a second straight month in May, declining by 29% to their lowest level since January.

Total sales dropped to 48,000 mt, down from 68,000 mt in April, and were 66% lower than the 139,000 mt recorded in the same month last year.

In other biofuel bunker news this week, Maersk Growth, the venture capital arm of A.P. Moller-Maersk, has invested in the two biofuel startups Vertoro and Kvasir Technologies. They develop technologies to convert lignin-rich biomass into marine fuels.

Service Terminal Rotterdam (STR) plans to build biofuel storage facilities in the Port of Rotterdam. It will build new storage tanks with a combined capacity of 100,000 cbm, capable of storing biofuels, as well as methanol and ethanol. The facility will be located adjacent to STR’s existing 240,000-cbm fuel oil terminal.

text:
EMA Group, an international group headquartered in Athens, Greece, is seeing strong momentum around carbon capture, utilization and storage solutions, as the shipping industry continues to explore practical pathways towards decarbonization.

Speaking during the event, Alberto Di Ceccio, Head of CCUS for Erma Tech Group, highlighted the strong attendance and the increasing interest from shipowners, design companies and industry stakeholders in green technologies.

“This year the attendance is amazing. Many people, many shipowners, design companies, you name it, and the interest for green technologies is spiking,” he said. “Everybody is looking forward to more decisions, hopefully in the next months. We feel the appetite for green solutions, not only for technologies, which is exactly what we are willing to offer on the market.”

Di Ceccio also presented CarbonFit, EMA Group’s technology designed to capture CO₂ from exhaust gases on board ships. According to him, the solution has been developed specifically for the shipping industry, with the needs of vessels taken into account from the very beginning.

“This is the logo of our technology, CarbonFit, for capturing CO₂ from exhaust gases of ships,” he explained. “It has been specifically enabled for the shipping industry around four and a half years ago, and it is still under refinement and improvement.”

He added that the company has focused on key operational requirements for vessels, including compactness, flexibility and ease of operation.

“From the very beginning, we kept in mind what is needed on a ship: compactness, flexibility and easiness of operation,” Di Ceccio said. “It is a peculiar technology. We put a lot of money, time and energy into it.”

Looking ahead, EMA Group expects the market for such solutions to accelerate as regulatory pressure increases.

“We really look forward to the start of the market, hopefully in 2027, with the new decarbonization rules,” Riccigno concluded.

The company invited industry stakeholders to visit its booth and discuss the future of decarbonization in shipping.

title: Maritime organisations call to include shipping in Electrification Action Plan
description:
On July 15, the Commission will publish its Electrification Action Plan (EAP), a crucial opportunity to accelerate electrification across Europe, cut fossil fuel imports, and slash both air pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions.
To maximise this impact, the shipping industry must be fully integrated into the plan.
In ports, shoreside electricity is already being deployed to connect ships to local grids, and daily port operations are steadily electrifying.
At sea, battery-electric vessels are becoming increasingly viable, with a growing number of electric ferries already sailing European waters.
